{{Short description|Greek mathematician (1872–1942)}}
[[file:Nikolaus Hatzidakis.jpg|thumb|right|250px]]
'''Nikolaos J. Hatzidakis''' (Νικόλαος Χατζιδάκις, also ''Nicholas Hadzidakis'', 25 April 1872 – 25 January 1942) was a Greek mathematician.<ref>{{cite web|author=Rassias, Themistocles M.|authorlink=Themistocles M. Rassias|title=The Greek Mathematical Society|website=European Mathematical Society (newsletter) September 2004|pages=34–35|url=http://www.emis.de/newsletter/current/current14.pdf}}</ref>

==Biography==
Hatzidakis was born in 1872 in Berlin. His parents were from [[Crete]]. He attended secondary school in Athens and studied mathematics at the [[National Technical University of Athens]] where he was awarded a Ph.D. in mathematics. He continued his studies in Paris, Gothenburg and Berlin.

He returned to Greece and was appointed professor of theoretical mechanics and astronomy at the [[Hellenic Military Academy]], where he taught from 1900 to 1904. He was a professor ordinarius of mathematics at the [[University of Athens]] from 1904 until his retirement in 1939 as professor emeritus.<ref name=Georgiadou>{{cite book|author=Georgiadou, Maria|title=Constantin Carthéodory: Mathematics and Politics in Turbulent Times|page=559|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=2004|isbn=978-3-642-18562-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lpprCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA559}}</ref> He also taught at the [[Hellenic Naval Academy]].

He was an internationally recognized expert on the mathematics of the kinematic equations of surfaces and was a founding member of the [[Hellenic Mathematical Society]]. He was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1912 at Cambridge UK,<ref>{{cite book|author=Hatzidakis, Nicholas|chapter=On pairs of Frenetian trihedra|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the Fifth International Congress of Mathematicians (Cambridge, 22–28 August 1912)|pages=138–143|volume=2|url=http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1912.2/Main/icm1912.2.0138.0143.ocr.pdf}}</ref> in 1920 at Strasbourg,<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Proceedings/ICM1920/ICM1920.ocr.pdf|pages=459–466|year=1921|title=Compte rendu du Congrès international des mathématiciens tenu à Strasbourg du 22 au 30 Septembre 1920|chapter=''Sur quelques formulas de géométrie cinématique'' by N. Hatzidakis}}</ref> in 1928 at Bologna,<ref>{{cite book|author=Hatzidakis, N.|url=http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1928.3/Main/icm1928.3.0439.0442.ocr.pdf|volume=3|chapter=Due proposte per l'insegnamento medio|title=''In:'' Atti del Congresso Internazionale dei Matematici: Bologna del 3 al 10 de settembre di 1928|pages=439–442|year=1929}}</ref> and in 1932 in Zurich.

Nikolaos Hatzidakis was a dedicated Greek patriot. In 1897 during the [[Greco-Turkish War (1897)|Greco-Turkish War]], he interrupted his studies in Paris to take part in the [[Cretan Revolt (1897)|rebellion]] against Ottoman rule that had begun in his family's homeland of Crete. During the [[Axis occupation of Greece]] in World War II, although he knew German and Italian, he did not cooperate with the occupying powers and died of starvation in the [[Great Famine (Greece)|Great Famine]], on 25 January 1942 in Athens.<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Hatzidakis|title=Nikolaos I Hatzidakis}}</ref>

His brother was the linguist [[Georgios Hatzidakis]] and his daughter was the writer, translator and critic Foula Hatzidaki (1906–1984).<ref>[http://www.kosmosnf.gr/2016/10/foula-hatzidaki/ brief remarks about Foula Hatzidaki - article by Costas P. Panteloglou {{in lang|el}}]</ref> Nikolaos Hatzidakis was interested in literature, linguistics and foreign languages. He published poetry in prestigious journals under a pseudonym and was said to speak thirteen languages. He published mathematical papers in Greek, German, French, English, Italian, and Danish.<ref name=Georgiadou/> His father was the noted mathematician [[John Hazzidakis|Ioannis "John" Hatzidakis]] (with the last name commonly transliterated as ''Hazzidakis'').
